name: PaySauce Limited
overview: PaySauce is a New Zealand-based cloud payroll SaaS and fintech platform for micro and small employers, covering rostering, mobile timesheets, payroll calculation, PAYE/STP tax filing, banking integration, digital employment contracts and an earned-wage-access feature (PayNow). Historically dominant in the NZ agriculture/dairy niche with roughly 8,600 customers at March 2026, the company spent FY2025-26 building a next-generation 'Global Payroll Platform' and, in April 2026, formally launched in Australia, a micro-business market it estimates is roughly seven times the size of New Zealand. It is a micro-cap (~NZ$39m market cap) listed on the NZX under PYS.

business_model.summary: PaySauce earns recurring revenue from two components it reports together as 'Recurring Revenue': processing fees (subscription/per-payslip fees charged to employers for using the payroll platform, PAYE intermediary and payments services) and interest income earned on customer payroll funds held in trust between collection and remittance to employees/IRD (the 'float'). Processing fees are the structurally growing, controllable line (+13% YoY to NZ$7.2m in FY26); interest income is exogenous to the business and fell 22% YoY to NZ$1.8m in FY26 as wholesale NZ interest rates eased, despite a larger float. Recurring revenue reached NZ$9.0m in FY26 (ARR ~NZ$9.0m, +6% YoY), with processing fees now 80% of recurring revenue, up from 63% in FY23 -- management frames this de-risking of the revenue mix (less reliance on rates) as a deliberate strategic outcome. Statutory 'Operating revenue' of NZ$9.2m also includes smaller other/subsidy revenue. Gross margin is stable at ~78%.

revenue_streams.name: Processing fees (payroll subscription + payments/PAYE intermediary fees)
Interest income on customer payroll float

business_model.customer_type: B2B, overwhelmingly micro and small employers (1-19 staff), historically concentrated in NZ agriculture/dairy but broadening into trades, hospitality, retail and general SME; distribution partly direct (search/content/advertising) and partly via bookkeeper/accountant and franchise/industry-association partner channels
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~100% of FY26 revenue (the funding engine); Australia commercially launched April 2026 (40 customers by 1 May 2026, pre-revenue scale); company references a historical presence across 14 Asia-Pacific jurisdictions via legacy/partner arrangements, though revenue is concentrated in NZ and nascent AU

main_competitors: Smartly (formerly SmartPayroll, PaySauce founder's earlier company)
In Australia: Xero, MYOB, Employment Hero, ADP, and fragmented spreadsheet/manual processes
competitive_position.market_position: A niche leader in NZ micro-business payroll, particularly agriculture/dairy where payroll complexity (variable hours, seasonal staff, awards-style pay rules) is high and larger platforms are weaker; a small player in the broader NZ SME payroll market where Xero (bundled with accounting) and Smartly have larger scale; a new entrant with no meaningful share yet in Australia (Forsyth Barr estimates <0.2% AU share in FY27)

moat_factors.description: Payroll is compliance-critical and historically sticky (average customer lifetime ~8.2 years, monthly churn ~1.0%); once IRD/ATO filing, banking and employee records are set up, switching is disruptive for a time-poor small employer

moat_factors.factor: Domain expertise in complex award/compliance niches
moat_factors.description: A decade of building payroll logic for NZ dairy/agriculture (seasonal, variable-hour staff) is being reused as a 'rules engine' to configure Australian awards (Pastoral, Retail, Hospitality) without rebuilding the platform -- a genuine, if narrow, technical edge over generalist competitors

Compliance deadlines (NZ payday filing historically, AU Payday Super from 1 July 2026) create forced software-adoption moments that favor purpose-built compliance products over manual/spreadsheet processes

High customer satisfaction scores (91% confidence in survey, NPS 44) and a service-led model (24/7 support, AI agent 'Penny' resolving ~80% of chat queries) differentiate vs lower-touch bundled offerings
PaySauce is far smaller than Xero, MYOB, ADP or Paychex; limited R&D and marketing budget versus incumbents that can bundle payroll for free or near-free with accounting software

weaknesses: Xero and MYOB can bundle payroll into a broader accounting suite already used by many small businesses, competing partly on convenience/price rather than payroll depth
Very small scale (NZ$9-10m revenue) versus global payroll players gives limited economies of scale in R&D, compliance monitoring, and marketing
Reliance on interest income (a declining, rate-sensitive, non-operational revenue source) has inflated historic growth optics
Thin trading liquidity (~NZ$7k/day turnover per Forsyth Barr) limits institutional interest and can cause outsized price moves

Unproven in Australia: pricing has already come in ~20% below initial launch assumptions, and management's own risk register flags partner-channel concentration (~60% of AU growth plan) and early-adopter bias

growth_drivers: Australian market entry: a micro-business TAM of ~694,000-700,000 employers, about seven times NZ; formal commercial launch 20 April 2026 with 40 customers by 1 May 2026 and management/Forsyth Barr guiding to a 2H27-weighted ramp

Australian Payday Superannuation reform effective 1 July 2026, requiring super paid concurrently with each pay run -- flagged by management (and independently by Forsyth Barr) as a catalyst comparable to NZ's payday-filing transition that historically drove software adoption

Migration of the NZ customer base onto the new Global Payroll Platform, expected to start later in 2026 -- an opportunity to lift ARPU/retention but also PaySauce's largest-ever operational change with execution risk

Consolidation of the fragmented NZ legacy payroll market as several smaller providers retire products, creating a 'once-in-a-decade' migration opportunity for accounting/bookkeeping bureaus to move client books to PaySauce

Revenue-quality shift in NZ: discontinuing the low-value 'Simple' direct plan and pushing customers to Standard/Premium, plus an April 2025 price increase, lifting ARPU and unit economics even as headline customer growth slows
AI-driven cost-to-serve efficiency (Penny AI agent resolving ~80% of chat queries, launched Dec 2025) supporting margin as the customer base scales
PayNow earned-wage-access feature as a potential incremental monetisation lever, within a fast-growing global EWA market

Partner-channel-led go-to-market in Australia (bookkeepers/accountants ~60% of plan; franchise/industry-association channel targeting ~85,000 AU franchise outlets with <20 staff) modelled on the playbook Xero used to scale in Australia -- reinforced by hiring former Xero Australia MD Chris Ridd and former Xero global partner lead Mel Shortland-Power

business.description: ~20% of recurring revenue (NZ$1.8m in FY26, down 22% YoY) comes from interest on customer float; this is outside management's control and fell as NZ wholesale rates eased through FY26 -- further RBNZ cuts would continue to pressure this line even as the float itself (customer funds held) grows

The core historical customer base and brand strength sit in NZ dairy/agriculture, a cyclical, weather- and commodity-price-sensitive sector; a downturn in farm incomes or seasonal labour demand could pressure NZ customer growth or churn
Small employers already using Xero or MYOB for accounting have a low-friction, often bundled payroll option; PaySauce must win on payroll-specific depth and service rather than price or convenience

business.risk: Slowing NZ growth during the AU pivot
business.description: FY26 gross new NZ customer additions fell 19% YoY (to 1,422) and CAC per addition rose 62% to NZ$944 as sales/marketing resources and management attention shifted to Australia; LTV:CAC fell from 12:1 to 7:1

Management's own risk register flags partner-channel concentration (~60% of the AU growth plan relies on partner recruitment/activation), strategic-channel (franchise/industry body) negotiation delays, and early-adopter bias in the initial cohort; advertised AU pricing already ~20% below original A$90 ARPU assumption

The planned staged migration of the entire NZ customer base onto the new Global Payroll Platform is described by management as 'the largest change PaySauce has taken on' and carries execution and customer-attrition risk (some legacy customers may not fit the target profile and may leave for alternative providers)

Founder-CEO Asantha Wijeyeratne (20.7% shareholder) has relocated to Melbourne to lead the Australian push personally; heavy reliance on his and a small leadership team's execution, though he has previously built and scaled a competing NZ payroll business (SmartPayroll/Smartly) successfully

financial.description: Market cap ~NZ$38-39m with average daily turnover of only ~NZ$7,000 (Forsyth Barr); thin liquidity means large buy/sell orders can move the price significantly and institutional participation is limited

PaySauce raised NZ$5m in a placement + oversubscribed SPP completed January 2026 (at NZ$0.26/share, a 7.1% discount) to fund the Australian expansion; founders sold down to fund/support the raise (CEO retained 20.7%, co-founder Troy Tarrant 9.4%); further capital raises are plausible if Australian scaling requires more funding, given forecast negative NPAT in FY27/FY28 (Forsyth Barr forecasts -NZ$2.1m and -NZ$1.2m respectively)

financial.risk: Margin compression during AU investment phase
financial.description: EBTDA fell 10% YoY to NZ$1.2m in FY26 and NPAT fell to NZ$0.3m from NZ$0.7m; sell-side forecasts (Forsyth Barr) model EBTDA turning negative in FY27 (~-NZ$0.9m) before recovering by FY29, i.e., a multi-year period of investment ahead of any Australian profit contribution
PaySauce pays no dividend and has signalled it will keep reinvesting profits into growth for the foreseeable future, so total return depends entirely on capital appreciation

regulatory.risk: IRD/ATO compliance and PAYE intermediary obligations
regulatory.description: PaySauce acts as a PAYE intermediary handling significant customer funds and statutory tax remittances in both NZ (IRD) and now Australia (ATO/STP); errors, security breaches, or licensing issues in this trust/payments function would be reputationally and financially damaging

regulatory.risk: Fair Work Act / award complexity in Australia
regulatory.description: Australian payroll compliance (Pastoral Award, Retail and Hospitality awards, upcoming Payday Super) is more complex than NZ; getting award interpretation wrong exposes both PaySauce and its customers to compliance risk during a fast market entry
As an FMC reporting entity, PaySauce carries standard NZX-listed governance and disclosure obligations

macro.description: The single largest identifiable swing factor in reported earnings; further RBNZ (and eventually RBA) rate cuts would directly reduce the float interest income line that still made up ~20% of recurring revenue in FY26

macro.risk: NZ/AU economic conditions affecting small-employer headcount
macro.description: PaySauce revenue scales with employee/employer counts processed through the platform; a broad small-business downturn or reduced hiring (especially seasonal agricultural labour) would slow processing-fee growth
As Australian revenue scales, currency translation and different pricing/cost dynamics (A$ vs NZ$) introduce a modest new FX exposure not previously present

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Cloud payroll/HR SaaS for SMEs continues to grow steadily in both NZ and Australia, underpinned by ongoing digitisation of manual/spreadsheet-based payroll and periodic regulatory catalysts (NZ payday filing historically; AU Payday Super from July 2026). Earned-wage-access/on-demand-pay is a fast-growing adjacent fintech category globally.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - underlying employer count and payroll processing volumes are tied to SME employment levels and, for the historical dairy/agri niche, farm-sector conditions; software/processing-fee revenue is relatively resilient (subscription-like), but growth investment plans could be curtailed in a downturn
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High and direct - unusually so for a software company, because PaySauce earns ~20% of recurring revenue from interest on customer funds held in trust; falling wholesale rates (as seen through FY26) mechanically reduce this revenue line regardless of operating performance

recent_developments.event: Company continuing Australian commercial rollout post formal 20 April 2026 launch; quarterly market update (June 2026 quarter) reported 8,756 active customers and processing fees up 11% YoY to $1.9m for the quarter, with a stated internal target of NZ$10m ARR in Q1 FY27
Investor and media conference call presenting an Australian market entry update, led by CEO Asantha Wijeyeratne and AU Executive Director Chris Ridd

FY26 full-year result and Annual Report released; Forsyth Barr initiated/updated coverage with a broadly in-line result read-through, cutting its spot valuation slightly to NZ$0.32 (from $0.33) on softer near-term profitability, partly offset by raised medium-term Australian customer growth assumptions
40 Australian customers signed up across dairy, retail and hospitality sectors following the formal 20 April 2026 launch
Formal commercial launch of Australian operations, ending a six-month soft-launch/pilot period that began September 2025 in Victoria
Completion of NZ$5m capital raise (NZ$3.5m placement + NZ$1.5m SPP, issued at NZ$0.26/share, 25% oversubscribed) to fund the Global Payroll Platform and Australian go-to-market

Chris Ridd (former Xero Australia Managing Director) and Mel Shortland-Power (former Xero Head of Bookkeeping/Global Partner Community) joined to lead the Australian growth effort; December 2025 marketing capital raise launched
Launch of Penny, PaySauce's AI customer-support agent, now resolving ~80% of chat queries and positioned as critical infrastructure for the coming platform migration
Soft launch/pilot of the Global Payroll Platform with Victorian dairy farmers, validating the product ahead of the formal Australian commercial launch
Modest NZ price increase implemented across the customer base, plus discontinuation of the low-value 'Simple' direct-sign-up plan tier, in favour of a revenue-quality-over-volume growth strategy

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Report (27 May 2026) and July 2026 investor update

items.notes: Internal target flagged in company quarterly update following FY26 ARR of ~NZ$9.0m; growth expected to be driven by both continued NZ processing-fee growth and early Australian contribution

items.target: Weighted to 2H FY27, largest volume of new activity expected Q4 FY27 (Jan-Mar 2027)
items.notes: Board has explicitly agreed not to revise Australian targets upward before the scheduled mid-year re-forecast on 15 October 2026, to guard against early-adopter-cohort over-optimism

items.metric: Revenue / EBTDA / NPAT (broker forecast, not company guidance)
items.target: FY27E revenue NZ$10.6m; FY27E NPAT approx. -NZ$2.1m (normalised); EBTDA turning negative (~-NZ$0.9m) before recovering to positive by FY29E
items.vs_prior: lowered vs prior Forsyth Barr estimates on near-term profitability, offset by raised medium-term AU customer growth assumptions
items.notes: These are Forsyth Barr (paid/commissioned) analyst forecasts, not company-issued guidance; company itself gives limited formal quantitative guidance beyond ARR/customer targets and qualitative outlook commentary
Management has signalled continued reinvestment of near-term profits into growth (NZ and Australia) rather than dividends

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Shelley Ruha and CEO Asantha Wijeyeratne characterised FY26 as a 'transition year' and FY27 as the year the company begins to test the scale of the Australian opportunity, with three stated FY27 priorities: (1) executing on Australian customer acquisition, (2) sustaining the NZ business that funds the group, and (3) lifting operating discipline to scale profitably. Management explicitly flagged that lower wholesale interest rates are likely to continue weighing on interest income, that Australian revenue will 'build through the year rather than arrive all at once', and that some initial AU marketing/setup spend will run at lower efficiency while the team learns the new market.

bull_case: Large, underserved Australian TAM (~7x New Zealand) with a proven, decade-tested payroll compliance product now live and validated in a real operating environment, led by credible ex-Xero Australia management (Chris Ridd, Mel Shortland-Power) who know how to scale a payroll SaaS business there

A structural regulatory catalyst (Australian Payday Super, effective 1 July 2026) closely mirrors the NZ payday-filing transition that historically drove PaySauce adoption, creating a time-bound reason for AU employers to switch off manual/legacy systems

Revenue mix is de-risking: processing fees (the durable, controllable line) have grown from 63% to 80% of recurring revenue since FY23, and NZ core business remains profitable and cash-generative, funding the AU expansion without heavy external debt
Balance sheet strengthened by the January 2026 NZ$5m raise (net cash ex customer funds of NZ$4.5m at FY26-end), giving management runway to execute the AU rollout without near-term forced dilution

High customer stickiness (average lifetime 8.2 years, ~1% monthly churn, LTV:CAC still 7:1 despite elevated AU-entry CAC) and strong customer satisfaction metrics underpin a defensible, if niche, moat in compliance-heavy micro-business payroll
bear_case: Interest income (~20% of recurring revenue) is falling as NZ (and prospectively AU) rates ease, meaning reported recurring-revenue growth (+4% YoY in FY26) understates true underlying softness once rate effects are stripped out, and further cuts would keep pressuring this line

Australian execution is unproven and the company's own risk disclosures flag heavy reliance on partner-channel recruitment (~60% of the AU plan), franchise/industry-body negotiation delays, and early-adopter-cohort bias; advertised AU pricing is already ~20% below original assumptions, pointing to competitive/pricing pressure before scale is achieved

Profitability is set to deteriorate through the investment phase -- broker forecasts model FY27/FY28 normalised losses (~-NZ$2.1m/-NZ$1.2m) as customer acquisition and R&D costs run ahead of Australian revenue, which is only expected to build materially from FY28 onward

NZ core growth has already slowed (new customer additions down 19% YoY, CAC per addition up 62%) as resources shifted to Australia, and the looming full-platform migration of the entire NZ customer base carries real execution and churn risk described by management as the largest change the company has undertaken

Severe micro-cap illiquidity (~NZ$7k average daily turnover, ~NZ$39m market cap) and reliance on a small founder-led leadership team (CEO 20.7% holder, personally relocated to run the AU launch) concentrate both key-person and liquidity risk for investors
